proposal.utterance: What BFO category best fits 'the normative force of an obligation'?

entities.label: NormativeForce
entities.rationale: Normative force is the capacity of an obligation to compel or bind its bearer — it is internally grounded in the obligation (or in the agent bearing it) and is directed toward realization in behavior. This fits BFO Disposition: a realizable entity that is internally grounded and can be realized in processes. It is distinct from a Role (externally conferred) and from a Quality (a measurable property without a directedness toward realization). The existing class LegalObligation already models the obligation itself (as a Role/SDC); NormativeForce would be a Disposition that inheres in the bearer of the obligation, representing the obligatory pull or binding character that the obligation carries.

relations.rationale: NormativeForce is typed as a subclass of BFO Disposition (BFO_0000016), reflecting that it is a realizable, internally grounded capacity inhering in the bearer of a legal obligation.

Open question — this relation is offered tentatively. NormativeForce could be modeled as a sub-type or component of LegalObligation, OR as a distinct Disposition that inheres in the same bearer. The user should clarify whether NormativeForce is a property OF the obligation entity or a co-inhering Disposition in the agent. Flagged in open_questions.

open_questions: Should NormativeForce be modeled as a Disposition inhering in the agent/bearer of the obligation (i.e., the person obligated), or as a property of the LegalObligation role-instance itself? BFO requires SDCs to inhere in exactly one bearer, so the target of inherence matters.

Is 'normative force' intended to track the phenomenological 'pull' experienced by agents, the structural binding character of a norm in a system, or both? The answer may affect whether Disposition (internally grounded capacity) or Quality (stable measurable property) is the better fit.

Should NormativeForce be a subclass of the existing LegalObligation class, or a sibling Disposition that stands in a distinct relation (e.g., associated with LegalObligation via some RO relation) without being a sub-type of it?
Is there an intended distinction between the normative force of a legal obligation and that of a moral obligation? If both are in scope, a more general parent class may be warranted.
proposal.rationale_summary: The phrase 'normative force of an obligation' refers to the binding, action-directing capacity that an obligation has — the property in virtue of which it imposes a demand on its bearer. In BFO 2020, this is most naturally typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016): a specifically dependent continuant that is internally grounded in its bearer and is directed toward realization in processes (such as compliance behavior or deliberation). A Disposition is preferred over Quality because normative force is not merely a static measurable attribute but has a directedness toward realization. It is preferred over Role because Roles are externally conferred by social/institutional context, whereas the binding character of an obligation is grounded in the normative structure itself. The existing class LegalObligation already captures the obligation as a role-type; NormativeForce as a new Disposition class captures its force or compellingness as a distinct but related SDC. The proposed subClassOf relation to LegalObligation is marked uncertain and flagged for user clarification, since the precise bearer and the relationship to LegalObligation need to be settled before committing that axiom.
